Crime spiralling out of control

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
…what is the crime situation on the ground after 5 months of lock down?

Unique Selling Point:
This is a topic that affects each and every South African

Summary:
SAPS releases comprehensive crime statistics once a year and it makes for dismal reading. Thye also started with quarterly reports and this showed that crime is down 40% because of lockdown. However, since the easing of regulations, crime is back with a vengeance. It seems that crime is becoming more and more lucrative because of the inability of the police to fight crime. From media reports, it seems that it is up and that couriers are being targeted more. We take a look at what is happening on the ground with the help of a private security company.

Further information:
SAPS releases comprehensive crime statistics once a year and it makes for dismal reading. Thye also started with quarterly reports and this showed that crime is down 40% because of lockdown. However, since the easing of regulations, crime is back with a vengeance. It seems that crime is becoming more and more lucrative because of the inability of the police to fight crime. From media reports, it seems that it is up and that couriers are being targeted more. We take a look at what is happening on the ground with the help of a private security company. In addition to SAPS there are also private security companies operating on the forefront of crime, and some of the bigger ones actually work with the police on ops and assist and support them in many ways. (there are about 6000 private security companies in South Africa). The idea is to hook up with a company with high credibility that has links with the Police on the ground and to get their take on the increase in crime in South Africa. We suggest we work with “Special Ops99” a company operating in Randburg/Sandton. The CEO is willing to assist us in any way they can. We can send camera people to drive along on patrols and we can even have our presenter join them for a few hours on patrol. They will be the focus, but in order to get a more comprehensive picture of crime, we will also use CCTV footage of recent incidents, like the attempted kidnapping over the weekend that was captured on camera. We will also obtain other crime scene footage and CCTV footage from a variety of sources.

Special Ops had an operation with SAPS on Friday night and promised to take some footage for us. I have not seen it.

I sent a camera guy with them on Saturday night and he drove with them – they were asked to clean two illegal clubs on Friday night.

Next weekend some more operation with the Police are lined up – but that will be too late if the story goes out this coming Sunday.

NB: They know of many courier companies being targeted but are not directly involved.

I am still trying to connect with a courier company or will contact the industry role players.

Interviewees:
• Mark van Rensburg, CEO of Special Ops 99
• One of Mark’s operatives
• Dr Johan Burger or Rudolph Zinn on crime increasing
• Courier company or industry rep
• Parents of the child who was nearly snatched or hero who saved the child

Script:


V/O:
This was the seemingly peaceful scene at a small restaurant in Johannesburg before an unknown man suddenly jumped the restaurant railing and attempted to grab a little girl sitting at a nearby table. In a flash another man pounced on the assailant from behind and wrestled him to the ground.

A few minutes later the same man is seen, bound and lying on the ground, babbling incoherently to onlookers. He has since been identified as Naseem Slamang. He appeared before the Roodepoort Magistrates court on charges of assault and attempted kidnapping and the matter has been postponed for further investigation.

This heinous incident took place last week at this small shopping centre in Florida, Roodeport. The man who saved the little girl is Dishal Sooku, a 38-year-old father of two. He had just taken over as the new owner of the restaurant on the day the incident took place.
Dishal:
When he got to the railing and jumped over is when I got up too. Obviously to defend whatever was happening at that moment. But no one expected him to attack the child. I would have thought he was going for a cell phone or a bag or something, but not, not a little girl.
V/O:
Fortunately for the little girl, Sooku also runs a Jujitsu school, and with a lifetime of martial arts training, he was primed to assess the danger posed to the 4-year old.
Dishal:
So as soon as he jumped over the railing, I saw him reach for the girl with both hands and my instinct were: I need to save the little girl. As a martial artist you are trained not only physically but mentally as well. You train for situations to be in control, to be calm. And to control the situation was to control the perpetrator. And it was going through my mind: If I can control the perpetrator, whoever else was around, he would let go of the girl and they would be able to help this little girl.
V/O:
And that is exactly what he did – gaining control over the perpetrator before security took over.
LINK:
This is unfortunately not an isolated incident. Every day videos are posted on social media showing innocent people falling victim to crime in South Africa.
V/O:
This incident took place in Centurion in late August at a day care centre. In the CCTV footage, a woman is seen with a young child. A car arrives and stop just metres away from them and a man with a gun approaches her. He tries to pry her watch from her wrist and then hits her with the gun. He demands her ring as well. She takes off the ring and throws it to the ground.

The armed man kicks her in retaliation…..The assailant looks for the ring on the ground …..before his accomplice - the driver of the getaway car – finds it.
LINK:
These are just two of an alarming number of crime videos emerging every day on social media.
V/O:
And together with daily media reports, it seems that there is an above-average increase in criminal activity. But without updated crime statistics available, it’s difficult to get a true reflection of the numbers. The Police’s last quarterly report shows that between April and June – when the country was under stricter lockdown regulations - there was a substantial decline in criminal activities.
V/O:
Dr Johan Burger is an analyst at the Institute for Security Studies and says the drop in crime during lockdown was to be expected, but now, the situation is changing.
Johan Burger:
Let us not be deluded by the fact that, the crime reports in the first quarter of the financial year, shows huge decreases in our crime levels. This is not a true reflection of our current crime situation.
V/O:
He says as restrictions continue to ease, criminal operations are making a comeback and anecdotally at least, it seems the crime rate is already exceeding the levels experienced before lockdown.
Johan:
With a huge amount of job losses with the economic downturn, there is a new driving force as far as crime is concerned, that is deprivation, desperation, that is increasing. We will certainly see a huge, huge increase over the next few months and even the next year or two.
V/O:
Dr Burger says several academic studies have established that there is a discernible link between unemployment and crime. During lockdown three million job opportunities were lost in South Africa.

Special Ops 99 is a private security company operating in Randburg and surrounding areas. Shane Theunissen is the operations manager and he says they have seen a marked increase in levels of crime.
Shane:
So, during lockdown what we saw was your trio crimes were definitely down, but there was a spike in domestic violence that was alarming. Now that are at level 2 we’ve seen it go the other way where geo crimes have spiked and domestic violence is much lower.

Presenter:
When you speak about trio crimes, what crimes are those?

Shane:
So your armed robberies, your business robberies, your theft of motor vehicles, things like that.
V/O:
Mark van Rensburg is the CEO and he says the attempted kidnapping in Roodepoort could be part of a developing trend.
Mark:
Look I can’t factually tell you how many of these cases have happened, but it It has been brought to my attention over the last couple of months that there has been a couple of attempts of let’s call it kidnapping or someone trying to take a child. I do not have the exact stats or confirmation thereof, but those conversations are happening. And yes, the trend is definitely there.
V/O:
Van Rensburg says he is seeing elevated levels of serious and violent crime as well.
Mark:
Hijackings happen, we get to hear about it on a weekly basis. Where there has been a or to hijackings in an area, or a suburb or people have been followed home. We have experience of about one or two people a week that are getting followed home. The Rolex gang stealing a rolex, or a vehicle, or a lady with a fancy wallet. This happens relatively often as well, and ja I’d say it happens at least once or twice a week that we work with.
V/O:
It also seems that above-average rates of petty crime, brought on by increased unemployment, are being reported.

In this incident, an opportunistic criminal is caught on camera as he attempts to grab the cyclist’s bicycle. It happened in Hermanus a few days ago. Experts say that this is typical of many petty crimes which often occur on the spur of the moment.
Mark:
Well, what we see is that there are more and more petty crimes, where people will break in and steal the odd laptops, bicycles… those are on quite a regular basis. Opportunists are taking chances, grabbing a cell phone at a restaurant, these things happen on a regular basis, daily basis, hourly basis.
V/O:
Another consequence of increased unemployment is the growth of informal settlements in urban areas.
Theunissen and his team accompanied us to a new one taking shape just off William Nicol Drive – a very busy road in Gauteng.

Contrary to popular belief, Theunissen, believes that these informal settlements are responsible for only a tiny percentage of crime in the area.
Shane:
Ja, guys, it is a misperception that all of our crime is coming from here. This is not responsible the crime coming in to our affluent suburbs, all of our crime coming to theaffluent suburbs is coming from an outside area. They are not from these guys.
V/O:
It was here where I met with some young men who told me that they had lost their jobs during lockdown and have nowhere else to go. They now make a living through recycling.
LINK:
So, the interesting thing about the place is that there is a hair salon, but the hair salon is very safe, it as security cameras. You find that the community is trying to make means to survive. There are solar panels here and this is giving electricity and the music blaring in the background is obviously for the radio to be able to play. There is a tuck shop over here if you want to buy anything. There is a shebeen a place where you can get a drink after a hard day of pulling all the rubble and trying to make money out of waste. It is a community.
V/O:
As the value of cell phones increases, so do incidents of snatching. And criminals are becoming more brazen and are well organized. In this video taken in Centurion, a thief sneaks up behind an unsuspecting woman and snatches her phone away before jumping into the get-away vehicle.
Shane:
These people are in vehicles, nobody snatches a cell phone and runs 3 km’s home that doesn’t happen.
V/O:
Ferdi Gobey is a risk management specialist who works in the distribution industry. He says during the strict lockdown period far more people turned to online retail shopping.

Ferdi:
Where we saw them buying essentials, we can see that there is about a 70% increase in buying speciality items now on e-commerce. Normally the product gets ordered, it then gets into the distribution chain, it goes onto a light delivery vehicle, and it ends up with the consumer.

And criminals have caught on – targeting delivery vehicles filled with valuable goods purchased by online consumers. It’s resulted in a massive increase in vehicle heists like this one.

Unlike Cash in Transit vehicles, courier vans are soft targets. The delivery men are usually unarmed – and they certainly aren’t driving armoured vehicles.

Ferdi:
There is definitely a big spike in hi-jackings on the light delivery vehicles.


And organised crime syndicates are also back in operation because early phases of lockdown, with heightened police and military presence, saw their movement hampered.
Johan Burger:
Syndicates were also keeping a low profile during the worst of the lockdown, but they ended money, you know, to keep their extravagant lifestyles going. So, the moment the lockdown, you know, there was a relief there, of going down as far as the levels are concerned, immediately they started becoming active again.
LINK:
But now they are back with a vengeance and it seems they are making up for lost time.
Shane:
I deal with violent crime on a day to day basis, we’ve arrested a number of syndicates, a big syndicate, a Rolex syndicate that we arrested on the William Nicol about a month ago. We were involved in a big drug operation also on the William Nicol, with premises there, where we had a ground source that was feeding us information. For the past month we’ve been going and retrieving a number of narcotics, such as crystal meth and cat. That was a great one. We got some more criminals for cell phone snatching in Illovo. We’ve recovered stolen vehicles, so these are the types of things we are doing on a day to day basis.
Mac:
Advice to people in general about crime? From what you have seen and what your daily experiences are?
Shane:
Just be aware, be vigilant, and I think if you had to ask a hundred criminals what the biggest deterring factor would be it would be awareness and vigilance. Just be aware of your surroundings, you know. When you are approaching home, don’t be on you cell phone. Be aware of your surroundings, look in your rear-view mirror, make sure nobody is following you. If somebody is following you, go to your nearest police station. Just be aware, that is biggest deterrent for crime.
V/O:
And it was Dishal’s vigilance that saved the girl at the table and turned him into a social media sensation.
Dishal:
I do not consider myself to be a hero…..or I need something to protect this child.

There is a tuck shop over here if you want to buy anything. There is a shebeen a place where you can get a drink after a hard day of pulling all the rubble and trying to make money out of waste. It is a community. V/O: As the value of cell phones increases, so do incidents of snatching. And criminals are becoming more brazen and are well organized. In this video taken in Centurion, a thief sneaks up behind an unsuspecting woman and snatches her phone away before jumping into the get-away vehicle. Shane: These people are in vehicles, nobody snatches a cell phone and runs 3 km’s home that doesn’t happen. V/O: Ferdi Gobey is a risk management specialist who works in the distribution industry. He says during the strict lockdown period far more people turned to online retail shopping. Ferdi: Where we saw them buying essentials, we can see that there is about a 70% increase in buying speciality items now on e-commerce. Normally the product gets ordered, it then gets into the distribution chain, it goes onto a light delivery vehicle, and it ends up with the consumer. And criminals have caught on – targeting delivery vehicles filled with valuable goods purchased by online consumers. It’s resulted in a massive increase in vehicle heists like this one. Unlike Cash in Transit vehicles, courier vans are soft targets. The delivery men are usually unarmed – and they certainly aren’t driving armoured vehicles. Ferdi: There is definitely a big spike in hi-jackings on the light delivery vehicles. And organised crime syndicates are also back in operation because early phases of lockdown, with heightened police and military presence, saw their movement hampered. Johan Burger: Syndicates were also keeping a low profile during the worst of the lockdown, but they ended money, you know, to keep their extravagant lifestyles going. So, the moment the lockdown, you know, there was a relief there, of going down as far as the levels are concerned, immediately they started becoming active again. LINK: But now they are back with a vengeance and it seems they are making up for lost time. Shane: I deal with violent crime on a day to day basis, we’ve arrested a number of syndicates, a big syndicate, a Rolex syndicate that we arrested on the William Nicol about a month ago. We were involved in a big drug operation also on the William Nicol, with premises there, where we had a ground source that was feeding us information. For the past month we’ve been going and retrieving a number of narcotics, such as crystal meth and cat. That was a great one. We got some more criminals for cell phone snatching in Illovo. We’ve recovered stolen vehicles, so these are the types of things we are doing on a day to day basis. Mac: Advice to people in general about crime? From what you have seen and what your daily experiences are? Shane: Just be aware, be vigilant, and I think if you had to ask a hundred criminals what the biggest deterring factor would be it would be awareness and vigilance. Just be aware of your surroundings, you know. When you are approaching home, don’t be on you cell phone. Be aware of your surroundings, look in your rear-view mirror, make sure nobody is following you. If somebody is following you, go to your nearest police station. Just be aware, that is biggest deterrent for crime. V/O: And it was Dishal’s vigilance that saved the girl at the table and turned him into a social media sensation. Dishal: I do not consider myself to be a hero…..or I need something to protect this child.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): …what is the crime situation on the ground after 5 months of lock down?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: This is a topic that affects each and every South African
metadata.Summary: SAPS releases comprehensive crime statistics once a year and it makes for dismal reading. Thye also started with quarterly reports and this showed that crime is down 40% because of lockdown. However, since the easing of regulations, crime is back with a vengeance. It seems that crime is becoming more and more lucrative because of the inability of the police to fight crime. From media reports, it seems that it is up and that couriers are being targeted more. We take a look at what is happening on the ground with the help of a private security company.
metadata.Further information: SAPS releases comprehensive crime statistics once a year and it makes for dismal reading. Thye also started with quarterly reports and this showed that crime is down 40% because of lockdown. However, since the easing of regulations, crime is back with a vengeance. It seems that crime is becoming more and more lucrative because of the inability of the police to fight crime. From media reports, it seems that it is up and that couriers are being targeted more. We take a look at what is happening on the ground with the help of a private security company. In addition to SAPS there are also private security companies operating on the forefront of crime, and some of the bigger ones actually work with the police on ops and assist and support them in many ways. (there are about 6000 private security companies in South Africa). The idea is to hook up with a company with high credibility that has links with the Police on the ground and to get their take on the increase in crime in South Africa. We suggest we work with “Special Ops99” a company operating in Randburg/Sandton. The CEO is willing to assist us in any way they can. We can send camera people to drive along on patrols and we can even have our presenter join them for a few hours on patrol. They will be the focus, but in order to get a more comprehensive picture of crime, we will also use CCTV footage of recent incidents, like the attempted kidnapping over the weekend that was captured on camera. We will also obtain other crime scene footage and CCTV footage from a variety of sources. Special Ops had an operation with SAPS on Friday night and promised to take some footage for us. I have not seen it. I sent a camera guy with them on Saturday night and he drove with them – they were asked to clean two illegal clubs on Friday night. Next weekend some more operation with the Police are lined up – but that will be too late if the story goes out this coming Sunday. NB: They know of many courier companies being targeted but are not directly involved. I am still trying to connect with a courier company or will contact the industry role players. Interviewees: • Mark van Rensburg, CEO of Special Ops 99 • One of Mark’s operatives • Dr Johan Burger or Rudolph Zinn on crime increasing • Courier company or industry rep • Parents of the child who was nearly snatched or hero who saved the child
